items.name: Problem
items.docs:
Why the text was not copied.

- `NotAllowed`: the browser refused. Most often no click or key press led
  to the write, or the page did not have focus.
- `Insecure`: the page is not served over HTTPS (or from localhost).
- `Unsupported`: the browser has no clipboard to write to.
- `NotFound`: [Clipboard.write_text_of] was given a selector that matches
  nothing.
- `Other(name)`: anything else, with the browser's name for the error.
items.head: Problem

items.name: write_text
items.docs:
Put a text on the clipboard. Your message says whether it worked, so a
Copy button can say "Copied", or ask the user to copy by hand.

```roc
Clipboard.write_text("roc build", |r| Copied(r))
```

items.name: write_text_of
items.docs:
Put the text of an element on the clipboard: the element a CSS selector
matches. This is for text your app does not hold, like a code block in the
page around your app.

```roc
Clipboard.write_text_of("#install-command", |r| Copied(r))
```

The selector looks in your app's own view first, and then in the rest of
the page.

items.name: log
items.docs:
Write a line to the console.

```roc
Console.log("The app started")
```

items.name: show_modal
items.docs:
Open a `<dialog>` element as a modal: on top of the page, with everything
behind it out of reach.

```roc
UserClickedDelete => (model, [DOM.show_modal("#confirm")])
```

Render the dialog and what is in it from your model, like any element.
Only whether it is open lives in the browser, which is why opening it is an
effect.

The user can close a modal with Escape too. If your model keeps track of
whether it is open, listen for the dialog's `close` event:
`on("close", UserClosedDialog)`.

items.name: close_modal
items.docs:
Close a `<dialog>` element. Does nothing when it is not open.

```roc
UserClickedKeep => (model, [DOM.close_modal("#confirm")])
```

items.name: focus
items.docs:
Give an element the keyboard focus.

It runs after the view is up to date, so it can name an element the same
`update` just showed. The field is open and focused before the user's next
key press:

```roc
UserClickedEdit =>
    ({ ..model, editing: Bool.True }, [DOM.focus("#title")])
```

A text field gets its cursor at the end, so typing carries on from what is
there. Does nothing when the element cannot take focus, like a hidden or a
disabled one.

items.name: set_title
items.docs:
Set the page's title: the text in the browser's tab and in its history.

```roc
DOM.set_title("Inbox (3)")
```

An app with several pages returns it wherever it changes page.

items.name: scroll_to
items.docs:
Scroll the page to a position, in pixels from its top left corner.

```roc
DOM.scroll_to({ x: 0, y: 0 })
```

It runs after the view is up to date, so a page you just switched to starts
at the top and not where the last one was scrolled to.

items.name: on_document_click
items.docs:
A message when the user clicks an element that has a given attribute, or
anything inside one. The message gets the attribute's value.

```roc
DOM.on_document_click("data-copy", |id| UserClickedCopy(id))
```

It listens on the whole page, so it also hears the page's own HTML around
your app, which your app does not render and cannot put handlers on. When
several elements around the click have the attribute, the nearest one
counts.

items.name: Effect
items.signature:
[
	## JavaScript that answers (see Features in the runtime): its id as `Id`
	## marks it, its arguments (see Wire), on_reply. The reply is a status byte, 0 for done
	## and 1 for failed, then the answer (see Wire) or the reason as UTF-8.
	Call(Str, List(U8), Box((List(U8) -> Box(msg)))),
	## message drained to the browser console (see `Console.log`)
	ConsoleLog(Str),
	## JavaScript that answers nothing: its id and its arguments (see Wire).
	Send(Str, List(U8)),
]
items.docs:
An effect: something your app asks the browser to do, like make a request,
start a timer or change the URL.

Your `init` and `update` never do these things themselves. They return
effects, and Joy carries them out. When an effect has an answer, it comes
back to `update` as a message.

```roc
update : Model, Msg -> (Model, List(Effect(Msg)))
update = |model, msg|
    match msg {
        UserClickedSave => (model, [Console.log("Saving")])
    }
```

You rarely make an `Effect` yourself. The other modules make them:
[Http.get], [Time.after], [Navigation.push_url] and so on. What this module adds:

- [Effect.map] and [Effect.map_all], for an app split into pages or parts.
- [Effect.call], [Effect.send] and [Effect.reply], for a custom effect: a
  browser feature Joy lacks, with JavaScript of your own.
- [Effect.identity], for tests.

## Why an effect is a value

`update` only says what should happen. That keeps it a plain function: the
same model and message always give the same result. So a test can call
`update` and look at the effects it returned, with no browser.

The guide has pages on [effects](../../#effects) and on
[custom effects](../../#custom-effects).
items.head: Effect(msg)

items.name: map
items.docs:
Turn an effect of one message type into an effect of another. An app split
into pages uses it to wrap a page's messages in its own, so the answer
finds its way back to the page:

```roc
Effect.map(Console.log("Hello"), |m| SettingsMsg(m))
```

items.name: map_all
Id
items.docs:
The name of an effect's JavaScript, like `"my_app/share_link"`. It is what
the Roc and the JavaScript of an effect have in common.

You write it as a plain string where an `Id` is asked for. It has to be
written out in the code, not put together while the app runs: a build reads
the names out of your app to know which JavaScript it needs, and checks
that each one has some.
items.head: Id

items.name: from_quote
items.docs:
How the compiler turns a string in your code into an `Id`. You do not call
it. It refuses a name that is empty, longer than 100 bytes, or made of
anything but letters, digits and `_ - . /`.

items.name: to_str
items.docs: The name as you wrote it.

items.name: identity
items.docs:
For tests. What an effect asks for: its name and its arguments. A
`Console.log` has no name, and its text as its arguments.

```roc
expect {
    (_, effects) = update(model, UserClickedLoad)
    ids = effects.map(|effect| effect.identity().id)
    ids == ["joy/http/send"]
}
```

items.name: call
items.docs:
For a custom effect. Run your own JavaScript by its name, and get its
answer.

`args` is what the JavaScript reads, written with `Wire`. What comes back
goes through [Effect.reply], which says whether it worked.

```roc
get : (Try(Info, Str) -> msg) -> Effect(msg)
get = |to_msg|
    Effect.call(
        "my_app/locale_get",
        [],
        |reply| to_msg(info(reply)),
    )
```

The JavaScript is in the `.js` file beside the Roc module. The guide's page
on [custom effects](../../#custom-effects) shows both halves.

items.name: send
items.docs:
For a custom effect. Run your own JavaScript by its name, when it has
nothing to answer.

```roc
args = Wire.writer({}).u32(200).done()

Effect.send("my_app/vibrate", args)
```

items.name: reply
items.signature: List(U8) -> Try(List(U8), [EffectFailed({ name : Str, message : Str })])
items.docs:
For a custom effect. What your JavaScript answered, or why it failed.

- `Ok(answer)`: the bytes your JavaScript wrote, to read with `Wire`.
- `Err(EffectFailed({ name, message }))`: the error your JavaScript threw.
  A browser that refuses says `NotAllowedError`, and a name with no
  JavaScript behind it says `MissingEffectError`.

```roc
info : List(U8) -> Try(Info, Str)
info = |reply| {
    answer = Effect.reply(reply) ? |_| "The browser said no"
    (language, _) = Wire.reader(answer).str() ? Wire.explain
    Ok({ language })
}
```

items.name: Method
items.signature: [OPTIONS, GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, HEAD, TRACE, CONNECT, PATCH, EXTENSION(Str)]
items.head: Method

items.name: Header
items.docs:
One header of a request or a response, like
`{ name: "Content-Type", value: "application/json" }`.
items.head: Header

items.name: Response
items.signature: { status : U16, headers : List(Header), body : List(U8) }
items.docs:
What the server answered.

- `status` is the status code: 200 when all went well, 404 when there
  is nothing at that address, and so on.
- `headers` are the headers the server sent along.
- `body` is the content, as bytes. See "Reading the body" at the top of
  this page.
items.head: Response

items.name: Request
items.signature:
{
		method : Method,
		uri : Str,
		headers : List(Header),
		body : List(U8),
		timeout_ms : [TimeoutMilliseconds(U64), NoTimeout],
	}
items.docs:
Everything about a request, for [Http.request]. You rarely write one
from scratch: start from [Http.default_request] and change what you
need.

- `method` is `GET`, `POST`, `PUT`, `DELETE` and so on.
- `uri` is the address to send it to.
- `headers` are the headers to send along.
- `body` is the content to send, as bytes. `Str.to_utf8` turns text
  into bytes.
- `timeout_ms` is how long to wait for the answer:
  `TimeoutMilliseconds(5000)` gives up after five seconds, and
  `NoTimeout` waits for as long as the browser does.
items.head: Request

items.name: default_request
items.docs:
A request to start from: a `GET` with no headers, no body and no
timeout. Change the fields you need:

```roc
{ ..Http.default_request, uri: "/todos.json" }
```

items.name: method_to_str
items.docs: A method's name as text, like `"GET"`.

items.name: get
items.docs:
Make a `GET` request.

```roc
Http.get("/todos.json", |answer| ServerSentTodos(answer))
```

The second argument is how the answer becomes one of your messages.
The top of this page shows what the answer can be.

items.name: post
items.docs:
Make a `POST` request with a body. The body is bytes, and
`Str.to_utf8` turns text into bytes:

```roc
body = Str.to_utf8(Json.to_str({ title: "Buy milk" }))

Http.post("/todos", body, |answer| ServerSavedTodo(answer))
```

`post` sends no headers. To tell the server that the body is JSON, or
to use another method, use [Http.request].

items.name: request
items.docs:
A request where you decide everything: the method, the headers, the
body and how long to wait. Start from [Http.default_request] and change
what you need:

```roc
json = { name: "Content-Type", value: "application/json" }
body = Str.to_utf8(Json.to_str({ title: "Buy milk" }))

Http.request(
    {
        ..Http.default_request,
        method: POST,
        uri: "/todos",
        headers: [json],
        body,
        timeout_ms: TimeoutMilliseconds(5000),
    },
    |answer| ServerSavedTodo(answer),
)
```

items.name: post_file
items.signature: Str, U32, List(Header), (Try(Response, [HttpErr([Timeout, NetworkError])]) -> msg) -> Effect(msg)
items.docs:
Upload a file the user picked, with a `POST` request. The file is the
body.

A file input tells you about the file with `on_file` (in joy-html's
`Attribute`), and what it gives you has the file's `id`:

```roc
input([type("file"), on_file(|file| UserPickedFile(file))])
```

```roc
Http.post_file(
    "/upload",
    file.id,
    [],
    |answer| ServerTookFile(answer),
)
```

The browser sends the file straight from where it is. Your app never
holds its bytes, so a big file costs it no memory.

items.name: put_file
items.signature: Str, U32, List(Header), (Try(Response, [HttpErr([Timeout, NetworkError])]) -> msg) -> Effect(msg)
items.docs: The same as [Http.post_file], with a `PUT` request.

items.name: request_file
items.signature: { method : Method, uri : Str, headers : List(Header), file : U32, start : U64, len : U64, timeout_ms : [TimeoutMilliseconds(U64), NoTimeout] }, (Try(Response, [HttpErr([Timeout, NetworkError])]) -> msg) -> Effect(msg)
items.docs:
Upload a file, or a part of one, where you decide everything: the
method, the headers and how long to wait.

`start` and `len` say which bytes of the file to send, and a `len` of
0 means all the rest. Sending a big file a part at a time is how you
show progress, or go on after the connection dropped.

```roc
Http.request_file(
    {
        method: PUT,
        uri: "/upload/part/1",
        headers: [],
        file: file.id,
        start: 0,
        len: 1_000_000,
        timeout_ms: NoTimeout,
    },
    |answer| ServerTookPart(answer),
)
```

items.name: on_down
items.docs:
A message for every key that goes down.

```roc
Keyboard.on_down(|event| UserPressedKey(event.key))
```

items.name: on_down_keys
items.docs:
A message when one of these keys goes down.

```roc
Keyboard.on_down_keys(
    ["ArrowLeft", "ArrowRight"],
    |event| UserPressedArrow(event.key),
)
```

items.name: on_down_keys_prevent_default
items.docs:
Like [Keyboard.on_down_keys], and the browser does not do what it normally
does with those keys. Use it to keep Space from scrolling the page, or Tab
from moving the focus.

```roc
Keyboard.on_down_keys_prevent_default(
    [" "],
    |_| UserPressedSpace,
)
```

A key typed in a field outside your app keeps its normal effect.

items.name: on_up
items.docs:
A message for every key that comes back up.

```roc
Keyboard.on_up(|event| UserReleasedKey(event.key))
```

items.name: on_up_keys
items.docs:
A message when one of these keys comes back up.

```roc
Keyboard.on_up_keys([" "], |_| UserReleasedSpace)
```

items.name: on_up_keys_prevent_default
items.docs:
Like [Keyboard.on_up_keys], and the browser does not do what it normally
does when those keys come up. A key typed in a field outside your app keeps
its normal effect.

items.name: MediaStream
items.docs: An open microphone or camera, from [Media.stream].
items.head: MediaStream

items.name: MediaRecorder
items.docs: A recording that is under way, from [Media.record].
items.head: MediaRecorder

items.name: Problem
items.docs:
Why it did not work.

- `NotAllowed`: the user or the browser said no. Once refused, only the
  browser's own settings can change it.
- `NotFound`: there is no such device.
- `NotReadable`: another program holds the device, or the system blocks
  it.
- `Insecure`: the page is not served over HTTPS (or from localhost).
- `Unsupported`: the browser lacks the feature, or the format you asked
  for.
- `Other(name)`: anything else, with the browser's name for the error.
items.head: Problem

items.name: RecordingOptions
items.docs:
How to record.

- `mime_type` is the format, like `"audio/webm"`. `""` lets the browser
  choose: Opus in WebM where it can, and MP4 in Safari.
- `min_audio_bits_per_second` is the lowest audio quality you accept. A
  browser that would record lower is raised to it, and one that records
  higher keeps its own.
items.head: RecordingOptions

items.name: default_recording
items.docs:
The browser's own choice of format and quality. Start from it:

```roc
{ ..Media.default_recording, mime_type: "audio/webm" }
```

items.name: stream
items.signature: { audio : Bool, video : Bool }, (Try(Media.MediaStream, Media.Problem) -> msg) -> Sub(msg)
items.docs:
Open the microphone (`audio`), the camera (`video`) or both, for as long as
the subscription is in the list `subscriptions` returns.

```roc
Media.stream(
    { audio: Bool.True, video: Bool.False },
    |opened| StreamOpened(opened),
)
```

The browser asks the user first, so the message can come much later.
Asking for something else, like adding the camera, is a new stream: the old
one closes, and the browser asks again.

items.name: levels
items.docs:
How loud an open stream is, every `interval_ms` milliseconds. Use it for a
level meter or a live waveform.

```roc
Media.levels(stream, 50, |level| MicLevel(level))
```

The level is the loudest moment since the last message, from 0 for silence
to 1000 for as loud as the device can go.

items.name: record
items.docs:
Start recording an open stream.

```roc
Media.record(
    stream,
    Media.default_recording,
    |started| RecorderStarted(started),
)
```

A recording that is not finished when its stream closes is thrown away.

items.name: finish
items.docs:
Stop a recording and get it as a file.

```roc
Media.finish(recorder, "memo", |file| RecordingDone(file))
```

The file is named after `name`, with the ending of the format the browser
recorded in, like `memo.webm`.

items.name: audio_summary
items.signature: U32, U64, (Try({ duration_ms : I64, peaks : List(U16) }, Media.Problem) -> msg) -> Effect(msg)
items.docs:
The length of an audio file and its waveform, for a file the browser holds,
like a finished recording or a picked file.

```roc
Media.audio_summary(file.id, 200, |s| GotWaveform(s))
```

`peak_count` is how many points you want the waveform in. Each peak is the
loudest moment of its stretch, from 0 to 1000, and the stretches are spread
evenly over the file. The file's bytes never enter your app.

items.name: object_url
items.docs: A URL for a file the browser holds, to give an `

items.name: play
items.docs:
Play an `<audio>` or `<video>` element, found by a CSS selector. The
selector looks in your app's own view first, and then in the rest of the
page.

```roc
Media.play("#memo", |done| PlayStarted(done))
```

Browsers refuse to play sound before the user has clicked or typed
somewhere on the page. That comes back as `NotAllowed`.

items.name: pause
items.docs:
Pause an `<audio>` or `<video>` element.

```roc
Media.pause("#memo", |done| PlayPaused(done))
```

items.name: seek
items.docs:
Move an `<audio>` or `<video>` element to a position, in milliseconds from
its start.

```roc
Media.seek("#memo", 30_000, |done| PlayMoved(done))
```

items.name: navigate
items.docs:
Go to a URL by loading it, as a plain link does. Your app starts over, so
the model is gone.

```roc
Navigation.navigate("/login")
```

items.name: push_url
items.docs:
Change the URL without loading a page, and add a step to the history, so
Back returns to the URL before.

```roc
UserClickedLink(url) => (model, [Navigation.push_url(url)])
```

Your app hears of the new URL through [Navigation.on_url_change], the same way it
hears of Back and Forward. So the code that opens the page a URL names is
written once, there.

The page is then shown from the top, or from the element the URL's
`#fragment` names, as a page the browser loads is. Pushing the URL that is
already showing does nothing.

items.name: replace_url
items.docs:
Change the URL in place: no page load, no step in the history, and the page
stays scrolled where it is.

```roc
Navigation.replace_url("?q=${model.query}")
```

It is for things like keeping `?q=...` in step with a search box, where
Back should not walk through every key press. Your app hears of it through
[Navigation.on_url_change], unless the URL is the one already showing.

items.name: on_url_change
items.docs:
A message each time the page's URL changes. It carries the whole address,
like `https://example.com/notes/3?sort=new#top`.

```roc
Navigation.on_url_change(|url| UrlChanged(url))
```

It hears all of these:

- Back and Forward.
- [Navigation.push_url] and [Navigation.replace_url].
- A click on a link to a `#fragment` of the page, which the browser follows
  without loading anything.

An app with several pages opens the page an address names here, and nowhere
else.

items.name: on_link_click
items.docs:
A message each time the user clicks a link of your site inside your app,
with the link's whole address. Your app then decides what happens, and
[Navigation.push_url] with that address goes there without loading a page.

```roc
Navigation.on_link_click(|url| UserClickedLink(url))
```

Some clicks stay the browser's: one with Ctrl, Shift, Alt or Meta held, a
link that opens in another tab or downloads, and a link to another site.

Without this subscription every link loads its page, as links do.

items.name: listen
items.docs:
Listen to a port. Every text JavaScript sends on it becomes a message, for
as long as the subscription is in the list `subscriptions` returns.

```roc
Port.listen("price", |text| PriceChanged(text))
```

items.name: send
items.docs:
Send a text on a port.

```roc
Port.send("level", "9")
```

items.name: Sub
items.signature: { id : Str, args : List(U8), on_event : Box((List(U8) -> Box(msg))) }
items.docs:
A subscription: something your app listens to for a while, like the clock,
the keyboard or a port.

`subscriptions` looks at the model and returns what your app wants to hear
right now. Joy starts what is new in the list and stops what is gone. So to
stop listening, leave it out:

```roc
subscriptions : Model -> List(Sub(Msg))
subscriptions = |model|
    if model.paused {
        []
    } else {
        [Time.every(1000, |now| Tick(now))]
    }
```

You rarely make a `Sub` yourself. The other modules make them:
[Time.every], [Keyboard.on_down], [Port.listen], [Navigation.on_url_change] and
[Media.stream]. What this module adds:

- [Sub.map] and [Sub.map_all], for an app split into pages or parts.
- [Sub.KeyEvent], what a key handler gets.
- [Sub.listen], for a custom effect: a browser feature Joy lacks, with
  JavaScript of your own.
- [Sub.identity] and [Sub.deliver], for tests.

## When a subscription starts over

A subscription is known by what it listens to, not by the function you give
it. `Time.every(1000, ...)` is the same timer on every call, and it keeps
running. Change the 1000 to 500 and the old timer stops and a new one
starts.

Two subscriptions to the same thing share it, and each event gives both of
them a message.

The guide has [a page on subscriptions](../../#subscriptions).
items.head: Sub(msg)

items.name: KeyEvent
items.signature:
{
		key : Str,
		code : Str,
		ctrl : Bool,
		shift : Bool,
		alt : Bool,
		meta : Bool,
		repeat : Bool,
		is_composing : Bool,
	}
items.docs:
What a key handler gets about a key press. The subscriptions in `Keyboard`
hand you one, and so do the key handlers in joy-html's `Attribute`.

- `key`: what the key means, like `"a"`, `"Enter"` or `"Escape"`. It
  follows the keyboard layout and Shift, so with Shift held `"a"` arrives
  as `"A"`.
- `code`: which physical key it was, like `"KeyA"` or `"Space"`. It ignores
  the layout and Shift, which is what controls like WASD want.
- `ctrl`, `shift`, `alt`, `meta`: whether that key was held at the time. A
  Ctrl+S shortcut is `event.ctrl and event.key == "s"`.
- `repeat`: true for the repeats a held key sends. Skip those to react once
  for each press.
- `is_composing`: true while the user puts a character together from
  several key presses, as input methods for Chinese, Japanese and Korean
  do. Skip those to ignore the steps in between.
items.head: KeyEvent

items.name: map
items.docs:
Turn a subscription of one message type into one of another. An app split
into pages uses it to wrap a page's messages in its own:

```roc
Sub.map(Time.every(1000, |now| Tick(now)), |m| ClockMsg(m))
```

The subscription listens to the same thing as before, so it keeps running.

items.name: map_all
items.docs:
[Sub.map] for a whole list, as a page's subscriptions become the app's:

```roc
subscriptions = |model|
    Sub.map_all(
        Clock.subscriptions(model.clock),
        |m| ClockMsg(m),
    )
```

items.name: Id
items.docs:
The name of a subscription's JavaScript, like `"my_app/network_changes"`.

You write it as a plain string where an `Id` is asked for. It has to be
written out in the code, not put together while the app runs: a build reads
the names out of your app to know which JavaScript it needs.
items.head: Id

items.name: from_quote
items.docs:
How the compiler turns a string in your code into an `Id`. You do not call
it. It refuses a name that is empty, longer than 100 bytes, or made of
anything but letters, digits and `_ - . /`.

items.name: to_str
items.docs: The name as you wrote it.

items.name: listen
items.docs:
For a custom effect. Hear the events of your own JavaScript, by its name.

`args` is what the JavaScript is started with, and each event's bytes go
through your function on their way to `update`. Both are written and read
with `Wire`.

```roc
on_change : (Status -> msg) -> Sub(msg)
on_change = |to_msg|
    Sub.listen(
        "my_app/network_changes",
        [],
        |event| to_msg(status(event)),
    )
```

The guide's page on [custom effects](../../#custom-effects) shows the
JavaScript that goes with it.

items.name: identity
items.docs:
For tests. What a subscription listens to: its name and its arguments.

```roc
expect {
    sub = Time.every(1000, |now| Tick(now))
    sub.identity().id == "joy/time/every"
}
```

items.name: deliver
items.docs:
For tests. Hand a subscription an event, the way Joy does, and get the
message it makes.

```roc
expect {
    sub = Network.on_change(|status| NetworkChanged(status))
    event = Wire.writer({}).bool(Bool.True).done()
    sub.deliver(event) == NetworkChanged(Online)
}
```

items.name: after
items.docs:
Send a message once, `ms` milliseconds from now.

```roc
Time.after(3000, |_now| NoticeTimedOut)
```

items.name: every
debounce
items.docs:
Send a message once, `ms` milliseconds after the last `debounce` with the
same key. Each new one starts the wait over, so of a quick run of them only
the last fires.

Search as you type is the usual case. Every key press asks for the same
debounce, and the search runs when the typing has paused:

```roc
UserTypedSearch(text) =>
    (
        { ..model, text },
        [Time.debounce("search", 300, |_now| TypingPaused)],
    )
```

Keys belong to the whole app, so use one per thing you debounce. In a
component you mean to reuse, start the key with the component's name.

items.name: cancel
items.docs:
Call off a waiting [Time.debounce] by its key, so it never fires. Does
nothing when none is waiting.

```roc
Time.cancel("search")
```

items.name: Algorithm
items.docs:
The kinds of hash Web Crypto can make.

`Sha1` is no longer safe for anything that guards against tampering. It is
here for systems that already use it.
items.head: Algorithm

items.name: algorithm_name
items.docs: An algorithm's name as Web Crypto spells it, like `"SHA-256"`.

items.name: digest
items.docs:
Hash bytes your app holds.

```roc
WebCrypto.digest(Sha384, bytes, |hash| GotHash(hash))
```

For `Sha256`, the built-in `Crypto.SHA256.hash(bytes)` does the same with
no effect.

items.name: digest_file
items.docs:
Hash a file the user picked, by its `id`.

```roc
WebCrypto.digest_file(Sha256, file.id, |hash| GotHash(hash))
```

items.name: digest_file_slice
items.signature: Algorithm, { file : U32, start : U64, len : U64 }, (List(U8) -> msg) -> Effect(msg)
items.docs:
Hash a part of a file the user picked. `start` and `len` say which bytes,
and a `len` of 0 means all the rest.

```roc
WebCrypto.digest_file_slice(
    Sha256,
    { file: file.id, start: 0, len: 1_000_000 },
    |hash| GotPartHash(hash),
)
```

items.name: to_hex
items.docs:
A hash as text, the way hashes are usually shown: two lowercase hex digits
for each byte.

```roc
WebCrypto.to_hex([222, 173, 190, 239]) == "deadbeef"
```

items.name: Problem
items.signature: [WireEnded, WireMismatch({ value : U64, wanted : Str, found : Str })]
items.docs:
Why a read gave nothing. Both mean that the Roc and the JavaScript of an
effect disagree on what is passed.

- `WireEnded`: the bytes ran out. The JavaScript wrote fewer values than
  the Roc reads.
- `WireMismatch`: the value there is of another kind than the one read.
  `value` says which one, counting from 1, `wanted` what the Roc read and
  `found` what was there.
items.head: Problem

items.name: explain
items.docs:
A problem in words, for you to read while you write the two sides.

```roc
(language, _) = Wire.reader(answer).str() ? Wire.explain
```

items.name: Writer
items.docs:
Writes values, one after another. Start with [Wire.writer], add each value
with the method for its type, and end with `done`:

```roc
Wire.writer({}).str("memo").u32(3).bool(Bool.True).done()
```
items.head: Writer

items.name: done
items.docs: The bytes written, to hand to [Effect.call], [Effect.send] or [Sub.listen].

items.name: Reader
items.signature: { bytes : List(U8), at : U64, read : U64 }
items.docs:
Reads values, one after another, in the order they were written. Start
with [Wire.reader]. Each method gives you the value and a reader for the
rest, or a [Wire.Problem]:

```roc
(name, rest) = Wire.reader(answer).str()?
(count, _) = rest.u32()?
```
items.head: Reader

items.name: remaining
items.docs:
What is left unread, as raw bytes. This is for bytes that were not written
through a writer, which have no marks to read them by.

items.name: writer
items.docs: A writer with nothing written yet.

items.name: reader
items.docs: A reader at the start of some bytes.

items.name: Attribute
items.signature:
[
	Boolean(Str, Bool),
	String(Str, Str),
	## decoder of the `FileInfo` record, fired when a file input's selection
	## changes. See `on_file`.
	FileHandler(Box(FileInfo -> Box(msg))),
	## event name, key filter (empty matches all), prevent_default,
	## stop_propagation, decoder of the `KeyEvent` record. See `on_keydown`.
	KeyHandler(Str, List(Str), Bool, Bool, Box(KeyEvent -> Box(msg))),
	## event name, prevent_default, stop_propagation, msg
	MsgHandler(Str, Bool, Bool, Box(msg)),
	## event name, prevent_default, stop_propagation, decoder of the
	## `PointerEvent` record. See `on_pointer_down`.
	PointerHandler(Str, Bool, Bool, Box(PointerEvent -> Box(msg))),
	## event name, DOM property to read off the event target, prevent_default,
	## stop_propagation, decoder of the property's stringified value. See
	## `on_property`.
	PropertyHandler(Str, Str, Bool, Bool, Box(Str -> Box(msg))),
	## root_margin, rearm_key, msg. See `on_visible`.
	VisibilityHandler(Str, Str, Box(msg)),
]
items.docs:
Attributes for HTML elements.

Most attributes take a string, like `class("btn")` and `href("/about")`.
Boolean ones take a `Bool` and only appear when true, like
`disabled(Bool.True)`. Anything without a helper goes through
`attribute("data-foo", "bar")`, and `data`, `aria`, `classes`,
`class_list` and `style` cover the usual dynamic cases.

Event handlers are attributes too, carrying a typed message instead of a
handler string: `on_click(Saved)` sends `Saved` to your update function,
and `on_input(|s| Typed(s))` builds the message from the input's current
value. The second one takes a function rather than a bare `Typed`
because Roc tag constructors are not functions. The everyday handlers
are also re-exported from the shorter `Event` module.

Values are escaped and names are sanitized when rendered, so a dynamic
string cannot break out of its attribute.
items.head: Attribute(msg)

items.name: PointerEvent
items.signature:
{
		client_x : F64,
		client_y : F64,
		page_x : F64,
		page_y : F64,
		offset_x : F64,
		offset_y : F64,
		button : U8,
		buttons : U8,
		ctrl : Bool,
		shift : Bool,
		alt : Bool,
		meta : Bool,
	}
items.docs:
The record `on_pointer` handlers receive, annotated as
`Attribute.PointerEvent`. `client_x`/`client_y` are viewport
coordinates, `page_x`/`page_y` include scroll and
`offset_x`/`offset_y` are relative to the element itself. `button` is
the button that caused a press (0 left or touch, 1 middle, 2 right),
while `buttons` is the bitmask of buttons held right now, which is
what move handlers want: `e.buttons != 0` means a drag is under way.
items.head: PointerEvent

items.name: KeyEvent
items.signature:
{
		key : Str,
		code : Str,
		ctrl : Bool,
		shift : Bool,
		alt : Bool,
		meta : Bool,
		repeat : Bool,
		is_composing : Bool,
	}
items.docs:
The record `on_key` handlers receive, annotated as
`Attribute.KeyEvent`. `key` is what the keypress produced ("a", "A")
or the name of a non-printing key ("Enter", "ArrowLeft"), so it
follows the keyboard layout and Shift. `code` is the physical key
("KeyA"), the one to match for WASD-style controls. `repeat` is true
while a held key auto-repeats, and `is_composing` is true mid-IME
composition, where the keystroke should usually be ignored.
items.head: KeyEvent

items.name: FileInfo
items.docs:
The record delivered by `on_file` when the user picks a file. `id` is
an opaque handle to the browser-held File object. `size` is in bytes
and `mime` is the browser-reported content type ("" when unknown).
items.head: FileInfo

items.name: map
items.docs:
Re-target an attribute to a parent message type by passing every
message its handler produces through `f`. This is the plumbing under
`Html.map`, apps rarely call it directly.

items.name: to_ssr_str
items.docs:
SSR text for one attribute, used by `Html.render`. String attributes
render as `name="escaped value"`, boolean ones as the bare name when
true and nothing when false. Handlers and visibility observers are a
client-side concern and render as "", which the caller drops. So does
an attribute Joy's client refuses to set (see `ssr_allowed`): the
server's page carries exactly what the client would.

items.name: value_of
items.docs:
The value an attribute list sets: its last `value` string attribute,
the one a client applying them in order would end on. `Html.render`
writes a textarea's value as its text, because HTML has no value
attribute for one.

items.name: string_of
items.docs:
The last string attribute named `name`, in any case, the way
`Html.document` reads a bundle root's `data-joy-bundle`.

items.name: without_value
items.docs:
The attribute list without its `value` string attributes (see
`value_of`).

items.name: stop_propagation
items.docs:
Stop the event here instead of letting it bubble on to ancestor
handlers: `on_click(Ignored).stop_propagation()`. This is what keeps a
click inside a modal from reaching the backdrop that closes it.
Ignored on anything that is not an event handler, and in SSR.

items.name: prevent_default
items.docs:
Suppress the browser's default action for this event:
`on_click(Navigate).prevent_default()` on a link keeps the browser
from following its href. On a key handler with a key filter only the
listed keys are suppressed. Ignored on anything that is not an event
handler, and in SSR.

items.name: stops_propagation
items.docs:
Whether this attribute stops the event at its element, the flag the
client runtime reads to decide on a stopPropagation call. False for
anything that is not an event handler. Exposed because the variants
are private to this module, so this is the only way a renderer or a
facade like `Event` can see the flag.

items.name: prevents_default
items.docs:
Whether this attribute suppresses the browser default for its event,
the flag the client runtime reads to decide on a preventDefault call.
Exposed for the same reason as `stops_propagation`.

items.name: sanitize_name
items.docs:
Strip every character that is not an ASCII letter, digit, `-`, `_`,
`.` or `:` from a tag or attribute name. A space or `>` in a name
breaks out of the tag however the value is escaped, and no quoting can
make it safe there, so it is removed instead. Applied by
`Html.element`, `attribute`, `data` and `aria` as the string enters
the tree, which covers both SSR and client rendering.

items.name: attribute
items.docs:
An arbitrary string attribute, e.g. `attribute("data-id", "42")`.
The key is sanitized (see `sanitize_name`).

items.name: boolean
items.docs:
An arbitrary boolean attribute, e.g. `boolean("hidden", Bool.True)`.
Rendered as present/absent (HTML boolean attribute semantics).

items.name: style
items.docs: Inline styles: `style([("display", "flex"), ("padding", "20px")])`.

items.name: classes
items.docs: A class attribute from a list of names, joined with spaces.

items.name: class_list
items.docs:
A class attribute from (name, active) pairs, keeping only the active
names: `class_list([("btn", Bool.True), ("hidden", is_hidden)])`.

items.name: data
items.docs:
A `data-*` attribute: `data("id", "42")` is `data-id="42"`. The name
is sanitized (see `sanitize_name`).

items.name: aria
items.docs:
An `aria-*` attribute: `aria("label", "Close")` is `aria-label="Close"`.
The name is sanitized (see `sanitize_name`).

items.name: for_
items.docs: The `for` attribute on labels. Named `for_` because `for` is a Roc keyword.

items.name: type
items.docs: The `type` attribute, as on `input([type("checkbox")])`.

items.name: lang
items.docs:
The document language, as `html([lang("en")])`. Set it on the `html`
element: screen readers and hyphenation depend on it.

items.name: accept_charset
items.docs: Renders as `accept-charset`, the character encodings a form accepts.

items.name: autocapitalize
items.docs:
Whether a touch keyboard capitalizes automatically: "none",
"sentences", "words" or "characters".

items.name: crossorigin
items.docs:
CORS mode for a fetched subresource: "anonymous" or
"use-credentials". Needed on `script` and `img` when you want error
details or canvas access for a cross-origin file.

items.name: decoding
items.docs: Image decoding hint: "sync", "async" or "auto".

items.name: download
items.docs:
Turns a link into a download rather than a navigation. The value is
the suggested filename, and `download("")` keeps the server's.

items.name: http_equiv
items.docs: Renders as `http-equiv`, for `meta` directives.

items.name: inputmode
items.docs:
Which touch keyboard to show: "numeric", "decimal", "tel", "email",
"url", "search" or "text". A hint only, it does not validate.

items.name: itemprop
items.docs: Microdata property name, paired with `itemscope` and `itemtype`.

items.name: itemtype
items.docs: Microdata vocabulary URL, e.g. "https://schema.org/Person".

items.name: loading
items.docs: Deferred loading for `img` and `iframe`: "lazy" or "eager".

items.name: max
items.docs:
The upper bound of an input's range. A `Str` because the bound follows
the input's type: "10" for `number`, "2026-12-31" for `date`, "23:59"
for `time`. See also `min`.

items.name: min
items.docs:
The lower bound of an input's range. A `Str` for the same reason as
`max`.

items.name: property
items.docs:
Open Graph and RDFa property name, as on `meta`. Unrelated to DOM
properties, which `on_property` reads.

items.name: step
items.docs:
The granularity an input's value must fall on. A `Str` because it
takes "any" as well as numbers, and because the unit follows the
input's type as it does for `min` and `max`.

items.name: title
items.docs:
The `title` attribute, which browsers show as a tooltip. For the
page title use the `Html.title` element instead.

items.name: cols
items.docs: Visible width of a `textarea`, in characters.

items.name: rows
items.docs: Visible height of a `textarea`, in lines.

items.name: colspan
items.docs: How many columns a table cell spans.

items.name: rowspan
items.docs: How many rows a table cell spans.

items.name: maxlength
items.docs: Longest accepted input, in characters.

items.name: width
items.docs:
Intrinsic width in pixels, for `img`, `video` and `canvas`. Setting it
with `height` reserves the right space before the image loads. For a
percentage or any other CSS length use `style` instead.

items.name: height
items.docs: Intrinsic height in pixels. See `width`.

items.name: tabindex
items.docs:
Keyboard navigation order. `0` puts the element in document order and
`-1` makes it focusable by script or click while skipping the tab
order. Positive values jump the queue and are best avoided.

items.name: autofocus
items.docs: Focus this element when the page loads. At most one per document.

items.name: checked
items.docs:
Whether a checkbox or radio starts checked. Read the live state back
with `on_check`.

items.name: controls
items.docs: Show the browser's built-in play and volume controls on `video`.

items.name: hidden
items.docs:
Hide the element from rendering and from assistive technology. CSS
`display` overrides it, so prefer `class_list` when you style it
anyway.

items.name: itemscope
items.docs: Start a microdata item, scoping the `itemprop`s inside it.

items.name: multiple
items.docs: Accept more than one value, on `select` and on `input([type("file")])`.

items.name: novalidate
items.docs:
Skip the browser's own form validation on submit, leaving it to your
update function.

items.name: open
items.docs: Whether a `details` element starts expanded.

items.name: selected
items.docs:
Which `option` a `select` starts on. Without it a rendered dropdown
always opens on its first entry.

items.name: on
items.docs:
Send `msg` when the named DOM event fires: `on("mousedown", Grab)`.
Never rendered in SSR.

items.name: on_click
items.docs:
Send `msg` when the element is clicked, by mouse, touch or by keyboard
activation on a focusable element.

items.name: on_submit
items.docs:
Send `msg` when a form submits, suppressing the browser's default
(which would reload the page and lose the model). Put it on the
`form` element and submission by Enter or a submit button both fire.

items.name: on_property
items.docs:
Send the message built from a DOM property of the event target when
the named event fires:
`on_property("change", "checked", |s| Toggled(s == "true"))`. The
property arrives stringified, so booleans read as "true"/"false",
numbers as decimal text, and anything missing, null or NaN as "".

items.name: on_value
items.docs:
Send the message produced from the event target's `value` when the named
event fires: `on_value("input", |s| UserTyped(s))`.

items.name: on_input
items.docs:
Send the message built from the control's `value` on every keystroke,
as `on_input(|s| NameTyped(s))`. For a value read only once the edit
is committed, use `on_change`.

items.name: on_change
items.docs:
Send the message produced from the control's `value` when it commits a
change. Reads `value` for every element type, so one handler on a radio
group receives the selected radio's value. For a checkbox's on/off
state use `on_check`.

items.name: on_check
items.docs:
Send the message produced from a checkbox's checked state when it
changes: `on_check(|now| UserToggled(now))`. Don't combine with
`on_change` on the same element: both bind the change event, and the
runtime keeps one handler per event, so the last one wins.

items.name: on_key
items.docs:
Send the message built from the `KeyEvent` when a keyboard event fires
on this element: `on_key("keydown", ["Enter"], |_| UserSubmitted)`. An
empty key list matches every key, a non-empty one only the keys listed
(matched case-sensitively), and `.prevent_default()` then applies to
just those keys.

items.name: on_keydown
items.docs:
Every key pressed down on this element, browser defaults left intact.
Chaining `.prevent_default()` here suppresses Tab and the browser's
own shortcuts along with everything else, so prefer a key filter:
`on_key("keydown", ["Enter"], to_msg).prevent_default()`.

items.name: on_keyup
items.docs:
Every key released on this element. Unlike keydown it does not repeat
while a key is held.

items.name: on_pointer
items.docs:
Send the message produced from the `PointerEvent` record (coordinates,
buttons, modifiers) when the named pointer event fires on this element.
Pointer events unify mouse, touch and pen input. Chain
`.prevent_default()` to suppress the browser default (text selection
while dragging, touch scrolling).

items.name: on_pointer_down
items.docs: A mouse button, finger or pen made contact. The start of a drag.

items.name: on_pointer_move
items.docs:
The pointer moved over this element. Fires whether or not a button is
held, so drag handlers should check `e.buttons != 0` first.

items.name: on_pointer_up
items.docs:
Contact ended over this element. A drag can also end outside it, so
pair this with `on_pointer_leave` and `on_pointer_cancel`.

items.name: on_pointer_leave
items.docs:
The pointer left the element (or was lifted, on touch). Dragging code
should usually handle this like `on_pointer_up`.

items.name: on_pointer_enter
items.docs:
The pointer entered the element. Unlike a bubbling hover event this
does not fire again as the pointer crosses into a child.

items.name: on_pointer_cancel
items.docs:
The browser canceled the pointer stream (e.g. it decided a touch was a
scroll). Treat like `on_pointer_up`.

items.name: on_file
items.docs:
Send the message produced from the `FileInfo` record when the user
picks a file in this `<input type="file">`:
`input([type("file"), on_file(|f| UserPickedFile(f))])`.

items.name: on_visible
items.signature: msg, { root_margin : Str, rearm_key : Str } -> Attribute(msg)
items.docs:
Send `msg` when this element scrolls into view, the usual way to load
the next page of an endless list. `root_margin` grows the viewport for
the check, so "200px" fires 200px before the element really shows.

The observer fires only on the crossing into view, so an element that
stays on screen after the re-render never fires again and the loading
stalls. Give `rearm_key` something that changes when you want another
check (the number of items shown, say) and the observer re-arms with
it. Keep it constant to fire once per crossing.

items.name: on_click
items.docs: Send `msg` on click.

items.name: on_input
items.docs: Send the message produced from the input's value on every keystroke.

items.name: on_change
items.docs:
Send the message produced from the control's `value` when it commits a
change. Reads `value` for every element type, so one handler on a
radio group receives the selected radio's value. For a checkbox's
on/off state use `on_check`.

items.name: on_check
items.docs:
Send the message produced from a checkbox's checked state when it
changes: `on_check(|now| UserToggled(now))`. Don't combine with
`on_change` on the same element, see `Attribute.on_check`.

items.name: on_touchstart
items.docs: Send `msg` when a touch starts on this element.

items.name: on_touchend
items.docs: Send `msg` when a touch ends on this element.

items.name: Html
items.signature:
[
	Text(Str),
	Element(Str, List(Attribute(msg)), List(Html(msg))),
	Keyed(Str, Box(Html(msg))),
	Lazy(Box(({} -> Html(msg)))),
]
items.head: Html(msg)

items.name: map
items.docs:
Use a view that has its own message type. Every message its handlers
produce goes through `f` on the way to `update!`, so a component can
own a Msg union and the parent wraps it:
`Html.map(counter_view(model.left), |m| LeftCounter(m))`.

items.name: text
items.docs:
A text node. The string is entity-escaped when rendered, so it shows
up exactly as written and never as markup.

items.name: lazy
items.docs:
Skip re-rendering a region whose inputs did not change. Wrap an
expensive part of the view and pass the model fields it reads:
`Html.lazy2(render_cards, model.users, model.category)`. While both
fields stay the same, the previous subtree is kept and `render_cards`
never runs.

Pass fields and not the whole model: everything you pass is compared,
so one unrelated field changing costs you the skip. The view has to be
a named function too, because a lambda written at the call site is a
new value every render and never matches. Same for arguments built
during the render, like a mapped list or an interpolated string. They
are safe to pass, they just never skip.

`lazy2` through `lazy8` take more inputs. Past eight, pass a record.

items.name: lazy2
items.docs: `lazy` for a view of two inputs. See `lazy`.

items.name: lazy3
items.signature: (a, b, c -> Html(msg)), a, b, c -> Html(msg)
items.docs: `lazy` for a view of three inputs. See `lazy`.

items.name: lazy4
items.signature: (a, b, c, d -> Html(msg)), a, b, c, d -> Html(msg)
items.docs: `lazy` for a view of four inputs. See `lazy`.

items.name: lazy5
items.signature: (a, b, c, d, e -> Html(msg)), a, b, c, d, e -> Html(msg)
items.docs: `lazy` for a view of five inputs. See `lazy`.

items.name: lazy6
items.signature: (a, b, c, d, e, f -> Html(msg)), a, b, c, d, e, f -> Html(msg)
items.docs: `lazy` for a view of six inputs. See `lazy`.

items.name: lazy7
items.signature: (a, b, c, d, e, f, g -> Html(msg)), a, b, c, d, e, f, g -> Html(msg)
items.docs: `lazy` for a view of seven inputs. See `lazy`.

items.name: lazy8
items.signature: (a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h -> Html(msg)), a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h -> Html(msg)
items.docs: `lazy` for a view of eight inputs. See `lazy`.

items.name: keyed
items.docs:
Keep a list item tied to its data when the list changes. Children with
no key are matched by position, so removing the first row shifts every
row below it and whatever the browser holds (typed text, focus, scroll
position, a running animation) stays behind at the old position. A key
makes those move with the item instead:

```roc
Html.ul([], model.rows.map(|row| Html.keyed(row.id, render_row(row))))
```

Key every child of the list rather than a few, and use something from
the data that is unique among siblings and survives a reorder, so not
the list index. The key itself is never rendered. Rows that are also
expensive to build can skip that too:
`Html.keyed(row.id, Html.lazy2(render_row, row, is_selected))`.

(Elm and Lustre put the key on the container. Here it goes on the
child, so there is no separate keyed container helper.)

items.name: element
items.docs:
Create an element with an arbitrary tag name. The name is sanitized.
Characters other than ASCII letters, digits, `-`, `_`, `.` and `:`
are stripped so a caller-supplied string cannot inject markup.

items.name: render
items.docs:
Render a tree to an HTML string (server-side rendering). Text and
attribute values are escaped, event handlers are skipped and void
elements render as `<tag />`. Inline `script` text is escaped like any
other text and so cannot run, while `style` text is emitted raw.

items.name: ssr_document
items.docs: A full SSR page: "<!DOCTYPE html>" plus the rendered tree.

items.name: JoyFiles
items.signature: { loader : Str, runtime : Str, wasm : Str -> Str }
items.docs:
The URLs of Joy's files a page loads: the loader's, the runtime's and
each bundle's wasm by the bundle's id. A server learns them from its
build's assets.json, and a Joy project's generated/ package makes the
record (`Names.joy_files`).
items.head: JoyFiles

items.name: document
items.docs:
A full SSR page that runs Joy bundles. Each bundle root, an element
with `data-joy-bundle`, gets its wasm's URL in `data-joy-wasm`, and the
end of the head gets the loader as a module script and hints for the
runtime and each bundle's wasm, so the browser fetches them alongside
the loader instead of one after another. The page names no file of
Joy's itself. A page without a root renders as `ssr_document` does.

A wasm hint is crossorigin because the runtime fetches the wasm with a
CORS request, and a hint in another mode would not be used.

items.name: option
items.docs:
One choice in a `select`. The label is a text child and the submitted
string is `Attribute.value`. Mark the current choice with
`Attribute.selected`, which is what SSR needs to render a preselected
dropdown.

items.name: script
items.docs:
Load JavaScript with the `src` attribute. Inline script text is
escaped like any other text, and browsers do not decode entities
inside `<script>`, so an inline script never runs.

items.name: select
items.docs:
A dropdown of `option` children. Put `Event.on_change` on the select
itself, not on the options: it reports the chosen option's `value`.

items.name: style
items.docs:
Style text is emitted raw, not escaped, so inline CSS works as
written. The one rewrite is `</` to `<\/` (the CSS escape for `/`), so
the text cannot close the element early.

items.name: svg
items.docs:
An SVG root. Inner SVG tags have no helpers here, so build them with
`element("path", ...)`. Camel-cased SVG attribute names survive
sanitizing, so `Attribute.attribute("viewBox", "0 0 24 24")` works.

items.name: template
items.docs:
Markup the browser parses but does not render or run until a script
clones it. Its children are ordinary `Html` and are escaped like any
other, so this is a holding pen, not a raw-markup escape hatch.

items.name: textarea
items.docs:
Give a textarea its value with `Attribute.value`, like an input:
`textarea([value(model.draft), on_input(|s| Typed(s))], [])`. The
client then keeps what it shows in step with the model, and `render`
writes the value as the textarea's text, which is how HTML carries
one. A text child only sets the initial content, which the browser
stops following once the user has typed. Whitespace inside the tag is
significant, so do not pad the text for readability.

items.name: use
items.docs:
Reference another SVG node by id, the usual way to stamp out a sprite
from a symbol: `use([Attribute.href("#icon-close")], [])`.
